title: Given an array of positive integers, determine whether it can be split into two subsets with equal sums.
shortTitle: Partition Equal Subset Sum: subset-sum DP
keyPoints: The array can be split equally if and only if the total is even and some subset sums to total / 2
Reduces to the 0/1 knapsack feasibility variant where each number is used at most once
Use a boolean dp array where dp[s] means the sum s is reachable from a subset of the numbers
Sweep sums DOWNWARD (from target to num) to ensure each number is used at most once
Time complexity is O(n * target) and space is O(target) with the 1D optimization
An odd total returns false immediately without any DP computation
To recover the actual partition, backtrack through a 2D table or maintain parent flags

s1_definition.oneliner: Total must be even, and a subset must hit total / 2; solve with a boolean DP array swept downward.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Partition Equal Subset Sum** – determine if a positive integer array can be divided into two subsets with equal sums (LeetCode 416).
- **Reduction** – equivalent to asking whether some subset sums to exactly total / 2, because the complement automatically sums to the other half.
- **0/1 Knapsack** – each number is used at most once. The downward sweep in the 1D DP enforces this.
- **dp[s]** – boolean indicating whether sum s is reachable from a subset of the numbers so far.
- **Complexity** – O(n * target) time, O(target) space.
s1_definition.analogy: An auditor at the National Bank of India wants to divide a set of settlement amounts into two piles of exactly equal total for a two-way reconciliation. If the grand total is odd, this is impossible. Otherwise she checks whether some combination of amounts reaches exactly half the total, because that half automatically leaves the other half behind.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Partition Equal Subset Sum: [1, 5, 11, 5]

  Total = 22, Target = 11

  dp[0..11] boolean array:

  Init:       [T F F F F F F F F F F F]
  After 1:    [T T F F F F F F F F F F]
  After 5:    [T T F F F T T F F F F F]
  After 11:   [T T F F F T T F F F F T] ← dp[11]=true!
  After 5:    [T T F F F T T F F F T T]

  dp[11] = true → a subset sums to 11 → can partition

  Downward sweep ensures each number used at most once:
  for (s = target; s >= num; s--)
      dp[s] |= dp[s - num]
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Partition Equal Subset Sum reduces cleanly to a subset-sum feasibility problem. The array can be split into two equal halves if and only if the total is even and some subset sums to exactly half the total, because that subset automatically leaves the other half behind.

The DP solution uses a boolean array where `dp[s]` means sum s is reachable. Initialize `dp[0] = true`, then for each number sweep sums downward from the target to the number, setting `dp[s] = dp[s] || dp[s - num]`. The downward sweep is the 0/1 knapsack trick that prevents reusing the same number.

At the National Bank of India, auditors need to split settlement batches into two equal halves for two-way reconciliation. The DP table determines whether an exact split exists in O(n * target) time, and the 2D variant with backtracking identifies which specific amounts go into each half.

The senior point is recognizing this as the 0/1 knapsack feasibility variant where weight equals value, and knowing that the 1D downward sweep optimizes space from O(n * target) to O(target). An odd total is rejected immediately without any computation.

Remember one sentence: check for even total, then use a downward-swept boolean DP to test if a subset reaches half.
